read: full: all 7 pages (abstract, introduction, related work, composition, construction, evaluation protocol, experiments, conclusion, references)
venue_now: arXiv preprint only: the file is arXiv 2507.04766v1, 7 Jul 2025, with no venue (p. 1); cited_set_resolution.md finds no venue as of 2026-10
what_it_is: A 500-problem physics benchmark in two parts: Phy_A, 400 static graduate- or olympiad-level problems, and Phy_B, 100 problems with a variation engine that perturbs the numerical constants in their LaTeX reference solutions to make variants with the same physical model (pp. 1-3). Items were collected from textbooks and exam papers, rewritten by DeepSeek-R1 with manual review, verified by one or two annotators who solved them, and paraphrased by an independent reviewer (p. 3). All answers are numerical, with the unit and number of significant figures specified, and are accepted within 1% relative error; a Phy_B problem counts only if every variant is solved (pp. 2, 4). Of 15 models, the best reaches 43.0% on Phy_A, and accuracy drops by 22.5% on average from static to dynamic Phy_B (pp. 2, 4).
domain: graduate- and olympiad-level physics: classical mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, quantum physics, electrodynamics, semiconductor and fluid mechanics, atomic physics (p. 3)
size: 500 problems: 400 static (Phy_A) and 100 dynamic (Phy_B, three variants per problem in this release); 15 models in Table 2 (pp. 3-4)
source_of_items: textbooks and exam papers (OCR, manual extraction and annotation), with scenarios rewritten by DeepSeek-R1 and manually refined, and every question paraphrased by an independent reviewer; Phy_B variants are perturbed from these (p. 3)
instances: static (Phy_A) and perturbed (Phy_B: numerical constants regenerated by an engine still in development; the preprint releases three variants per problem, p. 3 footnote 2)
has_gold_traces: partial: ground-truth LaTeX solutions exist and drive the Phy_B variation engine, but scoring uses only the final numerical answer (pp. 3-4)
evaluation: final answer: numerical, parsed by a LaTeX-based function and accepted when |y_hat - y*| <= 0.01 |y*|; a Phy_B problem is credited only when all its variants are correct (pp. 2, 4)
human_validation: Each question and its solution were independently verified by one or two annotators who solved it step by step; the DeepSeek-R1 rewrites were manually reviewed; symbolic derivations and numerical end points were produced and cross-verified independently (p. 3). No agreement figures, no validation of the answer checker, and no described check of the generated variants (the cross-verification concerns the base problems).
contamination_measures: perturbations: dynamic numerical variants (Phy_B); paraphrasing of every question by an independent reviewer; LLM rewrites of problem scenarios (pp. 2-3)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1: 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2: 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.' R-1 (July rebuttal): 'ABench-Physics (Zhang et al., 2025b) uses a 1% tolerance for physics reasoning.'
engtrace_use.explanation: S-P1 lists ABench-Physics among benchmarks that target 'advanced symbolic' understanding, but the paper says it 'focuses exclusively on numerical calculation problems' and sets itself against benchmarks that require answers as expressions, naming PHYBench (pp. 2, 5): 'advanced' fits (graduate and olympiad level, p. 3), but 'symbolic' contradicts the paper. The May text also omits its defining contribution, the dynamic Phy_B subset whose numerical constants are perturbed to expose memorisation (pp. 1-3), which is the closest physics precedent for EngTrace's generated, contamination-resistant instances. S-P2's 'theoretical physics' is loose for problems drawn from textbooks and exams that include semiconductor and fluid mechanics (p. 3). R-1 is accurate: answers are accepted within 1% relative error (p. 4).

suggested_wording: ABench-Physics (Zhang et al., 2025b) pairs 400 static graduate- and olympiad-level problems with 100 whose numerical constants are perturbed to generate variants, crediting a dynamic problem only when every variant is solved and grading numerical answers at a 1% relative tolerance.
facts_to_cite: Phy_A has 400 static graduate- or olympiad-level problems; Phy_B has 100 problems with an engine that perturbs the numerical constants in their reference solutions (pp. 1, 3).
All answers are numerical, with the unit and significant figures specified, and are accepted within 1% relative error (pp. 2, 4).
A Phy_B problem is credited only if all its variants are answered correctly (p. 4).
The best Phy_A accuracy is 43.0% (Gemini 2.5 Pro); accuracy falls by 22.5% on average from static to dynamic Phy_B (pp. 2, 4).
Each question was paraphrased by an independent reviewer to reduce overlap with pre-training corpora (p. 3).
The released preprint has three variants per Phy_B problem, and the engine is still in development (p. 3, footnote 2).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: generated numerical variants of a fixed problem structure, the idea behind EngTrace's templates, at a far smaller scale (100 problems, three variants each); a tight numerical tolerance (1%, against EngTrace's REL 0.002); answers with the unit and significant figures specified. Lacks: gold traces used in scoring and any step-level evaluation (final numerical answer only); engineering domain (physics); any validation of the evaluator; any described check of the generated variants.
notes: A 7-page preprint with no venue. The text says Table 2 reports 'four widely used' models, but the table lists 15 (p. 4). Phy_A was selected by screening for problems on which models give long responses with low accuracy (p. 3), so its difficulty is partly adversarial to the screened models. The May reference list misprints all 12 first names against p. 1 (e.g. 'Yifan' for Yiming Zhang, 'Jun' for Junbo Zhao). In the revision it belongs beside GSM-Symbolic-style generation, not under 'symbolic' understanding.
